paras: The 1888 Donaldsonville lynching was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a crowd that took him from a jailer near Donaldsonville, Louisiana, in mid-November 1888, after he was accused of assaulting an eleven-year-old white girl on a nearby plantation. The account, a special dispatch to the New Orleans Times-Democrat, was reprinted across the country over the next nine days under headlines such as "A Wretch Lynched" and "Black Flend Lynched."

According to the dispatch, dated Donaldsonville, November 15, the girl, described as a child "of respectable parents," was playing with her younger sisters on a plantation near the town on a Tuesday afternoon, which before that date was November 13. No copy named the girl, her family, the plantation or the parish.

A Black man, called in the papers only "a negro" and "the wretch," seized the girl, flourished a knife and carried her into a canefield. The screams of the younger children brought plantation hands, who in most versions caught him "in the act of outraging the child"; the Delaware Gazette's copy said "feloniously assaulting," and several copies said only that he was caught. He was then taken to jail.

That night, the dispatch said, "so great was the indignation" that about 200 persons attacked and overpowered the jailer, took the prisoner out and hanged him. The Washington Evening Post put the interval between his capture and the lynching at "six or eight hours." No paper gave the man's name, the place where he was hanged, or the name of anyone in the crowd.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry appears in the coverage, which ends with weekly digests on November 24.

The story traveled almost entirely as one wire text. Washington's Evening Star printed it on November 15 as a New Orleans special to the Times-Democrat under "Lynching in Louisiana," with a subhead describing "A Negro Who Attempted to Outrage a White Child." The San Antonio Daily Light ran it the same day as "Fiend Frustrated and Lynched." On November 16 it appeared in the Indianapolis Journal as "Negro Criminal Lynched," in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette as "Black Flend Lynched" and in the Wichita Eagle as "A Rapist Strung Up." The same day the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer headed it "A Brute Lynched," the St. Paul Daily Globe "Hemped into Eternity. A Negro Ravisher Strung Up by a Mob," and the Savannah Morning News "Lynched for Outrage."

Weeklies carried the text into the following week, including the Concord Independent Statesman, the Delaware Gazette and the Austin Weekly Statesman on November 22. An Ohio News-Herald and the Hickman Courier ran it as "A Wretch Lynched" on November 22 and 23, and the Charlotte Messenger printed it on November 24. Two news digests cut it to one sentence, reporting that a Black man "who assaulted a young white girl near Donaldsville" was captured and "hanged by a mob."

These headlines called the accused a "fiend," "brute," "wretch," "ravisher" or "rapist," and the wire copies gave the dispatch's account of the assault as fact without comment on the lynching itself. The one comment found came from the Washington Evening Post, which observed in an ironic paragraph that "civilization in Louisiana is losing its grip" because the man "was not lynched until six or eight hours after his capture."

Copies disagreed on the day: most, including the earliest, put the seizure on "Tuesday afternoon," while the Austin Weekly Statesman printed "Thursday afternoon" and the Chicago Citizen said the man was "captured on Thursday." The Kanabec County Times said he was "captured on the 15th." Because Thursday was November 15, the date of the dispatch itself, the Tuesday reading fits an afternoon capture and a night lynching better, and the Thursday versions appear only in later weeklies and digests.

The field was a "canefield" in most copies and a "corn field" in others, among them the San Antonio and St. Paul printings. Most copies counted the crowd at "about 200 persons," while the Delaware Gazette said only "a mob." The Evening Star's own headline and the brief New Orleans note in the Silver State described an attempt to "outrage" the child rather than a completed assault.

bases: A crowd of about 200 overpowered a jailer, took an accused Black prisoner out and hanged him (A1, A11, A13).

The prisoner was taken from a jailer by force and hanged by about 200 persons (A1, A11), in retaliation for an accused assault on a child, 'so great was the indignation' (A1); a mob of unstated size in A13.

Every detailed version is one Times-Democrat special from Donaldsonville (A1, A11, A13); the brief New Orleans note (A3) and the Evening Post's 'six or eight hours' (A6) agree on the core event but may derive from the same report.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the dispatch verbatim under headlines such as 'Lynching in Louisiana', 'Lynched for Outrage' and 'A Louisiana Negro Lynched'.
Headlines named the accused 'Fiend', 'Brute', 'Wretch' and 'Ravisher' and the dispatch explained the lynching by 'indignation'.
The Washington Evening Post's ironic paragraph, 'Civilization in Louisiana is losing its grip', remarked that the man was not lynched until six or eight hours after capture.

conflicts.note: The earliest and most copies say Tuesday; Thursday was Nov. 15, the date of the dispatch itself, and appears only in later weeklies and digests, so Tuesday is the better-supported reading.
